section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from October to December 1932 documenting political instability, military factionalism, and right-wing extremism in Japan. Key topics include high-level police crackdowns on right-wing assassination plots against government leaders and financiers, internal factional struggles between the Araki and Ugaki cliques within the Imperial Army, and the founding of Kenzo Adachi's fascist-oriented Kokumin Domei. Additionally, extensive diplomatic correspondence between Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson examines Japanese public reaction to the Lytton Report, anti-American propaganda, and the strategic presence of the U.S. Pacific Fleet.

subfiles.about: A clandestine nationalist military pamphlet attacking Count Nobuaki Makino and General Kazunari Ugaki for court intrigue, corruption, and betrayal of the Imperial Army.
subfiles.from: Osaka branch of the Meiko-kwai (Imperial Army Officers)
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of a pamphlet circulated by the Osaka branch of the Meiko-kwai denounces General Kazunari Ugaki and Imperial Household Minister Count Nobuaki Makino as enemies of the nation. It alleges that Ugaki conspired with Shumei Okawa during the March 1931 affair to seize the premiership and subsequently betrayed his associates to escape punishment. The authors accuse Makino of shielding corrupt factions, orchestrating the May 15 incident, and maneuvering to install Ugaki as head of a successor cabinet, calling for decisive national action against both figures.
subfiles.title: Meiko-kwai Manifesto Denouncing Count Makino and General Ugaki (Translation Enclosed with Tokyo Despatch No. 180)

subfiles.about: A confidential letter from Ambassador Grew analyzing Japanese domestic reactions to Manchukuo recognition and the Lytton Report, with an enclosed memorandum from the America-Japan Society's secretary.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew assesses the Japanese political atmosphere following the recognition of Manchukuo and the release of the Lytton Report, observing that internal agitation has quieted despite widespread press bluster. He relays significant conversations with Prince Chichibu and Ambassador Debuchi regarding Japanese anxieties over U.S. naval preparations, advising that Washington maintain treaty principles without provoking military hotheads. An enclosed summary of comments by Mr. Takeda of the America-Japan Society highlights the Army's psychological obsession with saving face and warns that foreign pressure only unifies the Japanese public behind the military.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson with Enclosed Resumé of Mr. Takeda's Comments
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A personal and confidential letter from Secretary Stimson approving Grew's diplomatic approach while firmly defending the retention of the U.S. Fleet in the Pacific.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Stimson concurs with Grew's diagnosis of American policy, confirming that the administration has deliberately refrained from public comment on the Lytton Report or Manchukuo recognition. However, Stimson rejects suggestions that the U.S. Fleet should be returned to the Atlantic to mollify Japanese opinion. He maintains that fleet disposition is strictly an American domestic decision and that maintaining the fleet in the Pacific exerts a wholesome restraining influence on both the Japanese military and the general public.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan

subfiles.about: An internal State Department memorandum identifying the Japanese text submitted by Hal O'Flaherty as the original pamphlet translated in Tokyo Despatch No. 180.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Laurence E. Salisbury), Department of State
subfiles.summary: Division officers note that the seven Japanese pages transmitted by Hal O'Flaherty of The Chicago Daily News represent the original text of the anti-Makino manifesto translated in Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 180 of November 5, 1932. The note coordinates internal routing and handling of the material within the Far Eastern Division.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Anti-Makino Pamphlet
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: A letter transmitting photographic reproductions of a seven-page Japanese political pamphlet published in Tokyo at the request of correspondent Junius B. Wood.
subfiles.from: Hal O'Flaherty, Assistant Managing Editor, The Chicago Daily News
subfiles.summary: Hal O'Flaherty forwards photographic enlargements of a seven-page pamphlet published in Tokyo, complying with instructions from correspondent Junius B. Wood that they be filed to accompany Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 180 of November 5, 1932. Pages 101 through 107 contain the reproduced original Japanese text of the nationalist publication denouncing Count Makino.
subfiles.title: Letter from Hal O'Flaherty (The Chicago Daily News) to Department of State Transmitting Japanese Pamphlet

subfiles.about: A brief letter acknowledging receipt of the Japanese pamphlet reproductions transmitted by The Chicago Daily News.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges with thanks the receipt of Hal O'Flaherty's letter of November 18, 1932. He expresses appreciation for the courtesy in forwarding the reproduction of the pamphlet published in Tokyo on behalf of correspondent Junius B. Wood.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Hal O'Flaherty
subfiles.to: Hal O'Flaherty, Assistant Managing Editor, The Chicago Daily News

subfiles.about: A special diplomatic report analyzing an article in Le Figaro by E. de Guichen advocating Western support for Japanese dominance in Manchuria, accompanied by the newspaper clipping.
subfiles.from: Warrington Dawson, Special Assistant, American Embassy Paris (forwarded by Chargé d'Affaires a.i.)
subfiles.summary: Warrington Dawson reviews an article by E. de Guichen published in Le Figaro on November 13, 1932, arguing that Western powers should cooperate with Japan and recognize its civilizing mission in Manchuria. The author asserts that Japan requires an outlet for surplus population and serves as a vital bulwark against the spread of Bolshevism in China. Dawson notes in his commentary that the article appears to be paid propaganda subsidized by the Japanese Embassy in Paris.
subfiles.title: Paris Special Report No. W.D. 1134: A Plea for Closer Collaboration with Japan

subfiles.about: An internal memorandum summarizing four diplomatic reports from Paris concerning pro-Japanese commentary and suspected propaganda in the French press.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury summarizes four recent reports submitted by Warrington Dawson in Paris regarding articles in Le Figaro and Le Petit Parisien. The articles include critiques of the Lytton Report by Dr. Legendre and arguments by E. de Guichen and Andrée Viollis defending Japanese expansion. Salisbury highlights Dawson's evaluation that the sympathetic articles were likely subsidized by the Japanese Embassy in Paris.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on French Press Reports Regarding Japan

subfiles.about: A diplomatic report transmitting and reviewing an article in Le Petit Parisien by Andrée Viollis examining Japanese demographic pressure and emigration to Manchuria.
subfiles.from: Warrington Dawson, Special Assistant, American Embassy Paris (forwarded by Chargé d'Affaires a.i.)
subfiles.summary: Special Assistant Warrington Dawson forwards an article by Andrée Viollis published in Le Petit Parisien on November 17, 1932, titled 'Under the Japanese Mask: The Overflowing Population and Emigration.' The article surveys Japan's rapid population increase, the failure of birth control programs, and resentment over the U.S. Immigration Act of 1924, presenting colonization of Manchuria as an unavoidable necessity. Dawson comments that the publication reinforces his conviction that the Japanese Embassy in Paris was spending substantial sums to cultivate favorable French press coverage.
subfiles.title: Paris Special Report No. W.D. 1142: The Problem of Japan's Emigration

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording a memorandum by Under Secretary William R. Castle, Jr., warning of a potential social crisis in Japan.
subfiles.from: William R. Castle, Jr., Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references a memorandum by Under Secretary Castle dated November 22, 1932, filed under decimal 894.51/390. Castle warns that Japan faces a perilous future due to a deepening social crisis that could take a communist, fascist, or mixed socialist orientation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/448 (Memorandum by Under Secretary William R. Castle, Jr.)

subfiles.about: A letter from Ambassador Grew listing recent political despatches and commenting on Japan's budgetary difficulties and moderate tendencies.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew writes to Secretary Stimson drawing attention to several recent embassy despatches, particularly reports on Japan's mounting budget deficits and moderate political tendencies. He observes that while significant segments of public opinion oppose military chauvinism, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the military clique will lose control or moderate state policies. A list of five enclosed despatches covers Japanese strategy before the League of Nations, budgetary strain, and North China policy.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A confidential letter from Secretary Stimson acknowledging Ambassador Grew's letter of October 22 and noting ongoing developments in the Far East and Geneva.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Secretary Stimson acknowledges Grew's letter of October 22 and confirms having read despatches 162, 165, 166, 169, and 170. He highlights Grew's conclusion regarding the persistence of military control and notes that the State Department continues to follow events closely both in East Asia and at Geneva.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording an intelligence report on the political situation in Japan by the American Naval Attaché in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Naval Attaché, American Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note indexes Naval Attaché Report No. 156, dated October 21, 1932, filed under decimal 793.94 Commission/558. The report assesses political developments and internal conditions within Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/449 (Naval Attaché Report No. 156)

subfiles.about: A confidential communication transmitting a Nanking intelligence cablegram on growing friction between extremist and moderate factions in the Japanese Army.
subfiles.from: Hawkling Yen, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Chinese Legation, Washington
subfiles.summary: Chinese Chargé d'Affaires Hawkling Yen transmits to Stanley K. Hornbeck a confidential cablegram from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Nanking dated November 25, 1932. The cable reports serious dissension between War Minister Sadao Araki and moderates like Kuniaki Koiso and Jiro Minami, as well as the protest resignation of Guards Division Commander General Renzo Okamoto over unpunished extremist plots. It suggests that deepening military rifts and severe financial difficulties could provide an opening for moderates to regain political power. Pages 127 and 128 provide duplicate copies of the covering letter and cablegram.
subfiles.title: Note from Chinese Chargé d'Affaires Hawkling Yen to Stanley K. Hornbeck Enclosing Nanking Cablegram
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: A formal letter acknowledging receipt of Hawkling Yen's note transmitting the Nanking cablegram on Japanese political affairs.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges with thanks the receipt of Hawkling Yen's confidential communication of November 26, 1932. He confirms receiving the copy of the cablegram from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Nanking concerning internal political developments in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Hawkling Yen
subfiles.to: Hawkling Yen, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Chinese Legation, Washington

subfiles.about: An internal State Department memorandum summarizing Ambassador Grew's report on the mass arrest of right-wing radicals and their plots to assassinate Japanese leaders.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury reviews Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 197 regarding the police raid of November 5, 1932, in which 150 right-wing conspirators were apprehended. Targets for assassination during the imperial maneuvers included General Ugaki, Count Makino, Premier Saito, Finance Minister Takahashi, Baron Go, Seihin Ikeda, and Baron Hiranuma. Salisbury emphasizes that the government's decisive action was backed by War Minister Araki and that the Japanese press and public have reacted with severe disgust toward pseudo-patriotic violence.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 197

subfiles.about: A comprehensive diplomatic despatch reporting the arrest of right-wing radicals plotting assassinations of prominent statesmen and examining public hostility toward terrorism.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the November 5 police raids in Tokyo resulting in the arrest of right-wing extremists led by Hidezo Toyama, Yoshio Kodama, and Rihei Okada, who planned to assassinate General Ugaki, Count Makino, Dr. Ikki, Premier Saito, Finance Minister Takahashi, Baron Go, Seihin Ikeda, and Baron Hiranuma. Grew notes that the operation was authorized at the highest levels by Premier Saito, War Minister Araki, and Foreign Minister Uchida to suppress dangerous reactionaries. In sharp contrast to the aftermath of the May 15 incident, the Tokyo press and public have expressed strong condemnation of extremist violence and pseudo-patriots.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 197: Assassination Plots

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording Tokyo Despatch No. 202 concerning political reasons for an impending change in the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references Despatch No. 202 from Ambassador Grew, dated November 18, 1932, filed under decimal 894.002/202. The despatch examines political rumors and underlying pressures pointing toward a potential collapse or restructuring of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/452 (Tokyo Despatch No. 202)

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch analyzing the instability of the Saito Cabinet, budgetary disputes, and factional rivalries between the Araki and Ugaki military factions.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew examines recurring rumors of an impending cabinet crisis, pointing out the inherent instability of Admiral Saito's coalition ministry. He details growing apprehension among business leaders over unprecedented budgetary deficits generated by military expenditures in Manchuria, alongside partisan maneuvering by the Seiyukai and Minseito. Furthermore, Grew highlights the intense friction between the dominant Araki faction and supporters of General Kazunari Ugaki, concluding that despite widespread dissatisfaction, the cabinet's opponents lack a viable alternative.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 202: Political Reasons for Impending Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: An administrative instruction from the Department of State directing diplomatic officers to prepare concise digests or outlines for lengthy despatches.
subfiles.from: Department of State (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs diplomatic drafting officers to prepare a carefully formulated digest or outline for lengthy despatches transmitting published articles or extensive memoranda of conversation. The circular explains that such summaries assist departmental officers in Washington in quickly determining the relative importance of reports and deciding whether immediate reading is required. Brief despatches where an outline is clearly unnecessary are exempted.
subfiles.title: Department of State Instruction to American Embassy Tokyo Regarding Preparation of Digests for Despatches

subfiles.about: An internal State Department memorandum reviewing the background, platform, and parliamentary strength of Kenzo Adachi's new Kokumin Domei party.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury analyzes a Reuter dispatch from Tokyo announcing the inauguration of Kenzo Adachi's new political party, the Kokumin Domei (National League). He traces Adachi's political machinations since his split from the Wakatsuki Cabinet in December 1931, noting that the new group holds about thirty Diet seats mostly drawn from the Minseito. Salisbury points out that the party's platform mirrors those of existing parties except for its advocacy of a Japan-Manchukuo economic bloc.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei

subfiles.about: A telegram relaying a Tokyo press report on the eve of the formal inauguration of Kenzo Adachi's fascist-style party, the Kokumin Domei.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson relays a Reuter report from Tokyo announcing that Kenzo Adachi's new party, the Kokumin Domei, will be inaugurated before 8,000 delegates. The party platform emphasizes a Far Eastern Monroe Doctrine, a Japan-Manchukuo economic bloc, and sweeping administrative and fiscal reforms. Members plan to wear blackshirt uniforms, and lieutenant Heigo Nakano claims that party adherents already number two million nationwide.
subfiles.title: Peiping Telegram No. 1371: Formal Inauguration of Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei

subfiles.about: A telegram transmitting a Reuter report on the formal founding convention of the Kokumin Domei and Kenzo Adachi's inaugural address.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister to China, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits a Reuter dispatch describing the formal inauguration of Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei in Tokyo, attended by 4,000 members wearing blackshirt uniforms. The party manifesto asserts Japan's right to legitimate development against international unreasonableness and social injustice. In his inaugural speech, Adachi advocated national economic control based on a Japan-Manchukuo bloc and urged constructive relations with Great Britain, the United States, Soviet Russia, and China.
subfiles.title: Peiping Telegram No. 1372: Inauguration Ceremonies of Kokumin Domei

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording Tokyo Despatch No. 218 reporting the arrest of young reactionaries implicated in assassinations.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note indexes Despatch No. 218 (Political Report No. 60 for November 1932), dated December 9, 1932, filed under decimal 894.00 P.R./60. The note records that the despatch details the arrest of young reactionaries, including sons of prominent figures, charged with past political assassinations and plotting new attacks.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/455 (Tokyo Despatch No. 218 / Political Report No. 60)

subfiles.about: An extract from an embassy political report reviewing the arrest of young extremists plotting assassinations during the Imperial Army maneuvers.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 218 details the arrest of approximately twenty young radicals and leader Yoshio Kodama for plotting assassinations during the annual Army maneuvers in Osaka. Targets included General Ugaki, Count Makino, Dr. Ikki, Premier Saito, Finance Minister Takahashi, Baron Go, Seihin Ikeda, and Baron Hiranuma. The extract notes high-level government sanction for the arrests and observes that public sentiment has decisively turned against terrorist methods.
subfiles.title: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 218: Arrest of Young Reactionaries in Tokyo

subfiles.about: A personal letter from Ambassador Grew discussing the suppression of right-wing terrorism, the abatement of anti-American agitation, and Japanese policy at Geneva.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports significant progress in stabilizing Japan's political climate, noting that the government and War Minister Araki have curbed terrorist activities by raiding Mitsuru Toyama's home and arresting his son. He explains that anti-American press agitation has largely ceased following interventions by Ambassador Debuchi and the Emperor, accompanied by personnel changes in the War Ministry press bureau. Assessing Japan's diplomacy regarding the Lytton Report at Geneva, Grew argues that coercive threats would only unite the nation behind the military, whereas patient moral pressure will best support moderate Japanese leaders.
subfiles.title: Personal Letter from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State
